summary: This experimental document defines a convergence layer for CCNx and NDN over IEEE 802.15.4 LoWPANs. It specifies a new frame format for the small MTU, changes to TLV header formats, new 6LoWPAN dispatch types and use of 6LoWPAN fragmentation.

plainLanguage.summary: Small wireless sensors cannot carry very large packets, and the way NDN and CCNx write their headers is wordy. This RFC describes a way to write the same information in fewer bytes, so more of each tiny packet is actual content rather than header.

questions: how does stateful compression work in icn
subtitle: Compressing NDN and CCNx messages so they fit in low-power wireless packets.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4 wireless packets carry at most 127 bytes, and the Type-Length-Value headers that NDN and CCNx use are verbose, so most of a small packet is header rather than content.
tldr.mechanism: ICN LoWPAN reuses the 6LoWPAN dispatch framework and rewrites the TLV encoding: a compact bit field says which optional TLVs are present, names are compressed by packing two lengths into one byte, and shared context replaces repeated values.
tldr.outcome: For the example name given in the document, compression saves 17 bytes, which is 43 percent of the uncompressed packet, and evaluations report lower message overhead, shorter airtime and lower power use.

today: RFC 9139 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document states that it was published in the IRTF stream of the RFC series and does not constitute an IETF standard, and that it will be revised to progress to the Standards Track once sufficient operational experience has been acquired.

sections.title: Why ICN Needs a Convergence Layer for Small Radios
sections.content:
The Internet of Things has been identified as a promising deployment area for Information-Centric Networking (ICN), as infrastructureless access to content, resilient forwarding and in-network data replication demonstrate notable advantages over the Internet host-to-host approach. Recent studies have shown that an appropriate mapping to link-layer technologies has a large impact on the practical performance of an ICN. This is even more relevant for IoT communication, where nodes often exchange messages over low-power wireless links under lossy conditions.

The IEEE 802.15.4 link layer is used in low-power and lossy networks, in which devices are typically battery operated and constrained in resources. Characteristics of these networks include an unreliable environment, low-bandwidth transmissions and increased latencies. IEEE 802.15.4 admits a maximum physical-layer packet size of 127 bytes. The maximum frame header size is 25 bytes, which leaves 102 bytes for the payload, and the IEEE 802.15.4 security features further reduce this payload length by up to 21 bytes, yielding a net of 81 bytes for CCNx or NDN packet headers, signatures and content.

6LoWPAN (RFC 4944, RFC 6282) is a convergence layer that provides frame formats, header compression and adaptation-layer fragmentation for IPv6 packets in IEEE 802.15.4 networks. It introduces a dispatching framework that prepends further information to 6LoWPAN packets, including a protocol identifier for the payload and meta information about fragmentation.

Prevalent packet formats based on Type-Length-Value, such as those in CCNx and NDN, are designed to be generic and extensible. That leads to header verbosity, which is inappropriate in the constrained environments of IEEE 802.15.4 links. This document presents ICN LoWPAN, a convergence layer for IEEE 802.15.4 motivated by 6LoWPAN, which compresses the packet headers of CCNx and NDN and so allows for an increased effective payload size per packet. Reusing the 6LoWPAN dispatching framework also enables compatibility between coexisting wireless deployments of competing network technologies, and allows reuse of the 6LoWPAN adaptation-layer fragmentation scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: Small wireless sensors cannot carry very large packets, and the way NDN and CCNx write their headers is wordy. This RFC describes a way to write the same information in fewer bytes, so more of each tiny packet is actual content rather than header.

sections.title: The LoWPAN Encapsulation
sections.content:
ICN LoWPAN provides a convergence layer that maps ICN packets onto constrained link-layer technologies, including link-layer fragmentation, protocol separation at the link-layer level and link-layer address mappings. The stack places the ICN LoWPAN layer between the NDN or CCNx layer and the link layer.

The IEEE 802.15.4 frame header does not provide a protocol identifier for its payload, which causes problems of misinterpreting frames when several network layers coexist on the same link. To mitigate this, 6LoWPAN defines dispatches as encapsulation headers for IEEE 802.15.4 frames. Multiple LoWPAN encapsulation headers can precede the actual payload, and each is identified by a dispatch type. RFC 8025 further specifies dispatch Pages to switch between different contexts; when a parser encounters a Page switch header, all following encapsulation headers are interpreted using the dispatch Page given by that header. Pages 0 and 1 are reserved for 6LoWPAN, and this document uses Page 14, 1111 1110 (0xFE), for ICN LoWPAN.

The base dispatch format is one byte with four flags. The first bit is 0. The P bit says whether the included protocol is NDN (0) or CCNx (1). The M bit says whether the payload contains an Interest message (0) or a Data message (1). The C bit says whether the message is compressed (0) or compressed (1). Frames with compressed messages use an extended dispatch format with two further bits: CID, which says whether context identifiers are present, and EXT, which says whether extension bytes are present.

Extension bytes allow the initial compression rule set to be extended. The base format for an extension byte has a single EXT bit in the last position, where 0 means no further extension byte follows and 1 means one does. Extension bytes are numbered according to their order, and future documents MUST follow the naming scheme EXT_0, EXT_1 and so on.

For fragmentation, ICN LoWPAN adopts the protocol-independent fragmentation dispatch type of RFC 4944, with a fragmentation header for the first fragment and a separate header for subsequent fragments. The fragmentation header can encapsulate other dispatch headers, and the reassembled frame contains no fragmentation headers. The 6LoWPAN Fragment Forwarding mechanism of RFC 8930 is an alternative that forwards fragments without reassembling packets on every intermediate hop, and by reusing the dispatching framework it integrates into ICN LoWPAN as seamlessly as the conventional hop-wise fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Every ICN LoWPAN packet carries a small header saying which protocol it holds, whether it is a request or a reply, and whether it is compressed. That header rides on top of the standard 6LoWPAN headers, so an ICN network and an IPv6 network can share the same radio without confusing each other.

sections.title: Stateless Header Compression
sections.content:
ICN LoWPAN defines a stateless header compression scheme whose main purpose is to reduce the header overhead of ICN packets, which is of particular importance for link layers with small MTUs. Stateless compression does not require preconfiguration of a global state.

The CCNx and NDN header formats are composed of Type-Length-Value fields. The advantage of the TLV format is its support of variably structured data; the main disadvantage is the verbosity that results from storing the type and length of the encoded data. The compression scheme uses compact bit fields to indicate the presence of optional TLVs in the uncompressed packet, with the order of set bits corresponding to the order of each TLV in the packet. Further compression is achieved by specifying default values and reducing the range of certain header fields. In the example given in the document, the type of the first TLV is removed and the corresponding bit is set, a fixed-length TLV such as the NDN Nonce TLV loses its Type and Length fields, and a boolean TLV such as the NDN MustBeFresh selector loses its Type, Length and Value fields altogether.

Two further encodings shrink the headers further. Compressed NDN TLVs encode Type and Length fields using self-delimiting numeric values, where a single bit indicates whether further bytes follow, instead of the NDN scheme where the first byte is a marker for the number of following bytes. For values up to 127 both methods need a single byte; from 128 to 252 the NDN scheme needs one byte while SDNVs need two, and from 253 upwards SDNVs need no more bytes than the NDN encoding.

Name TLV compression encodes the Length fields of two consecutive NameComponent TLVs into one byte, using a nibble for each. The most significant nibble gives the length of the immediately following NameComponent TLV and the least significant nibble gives the length of a subsequent one. A length of 0 marks the end of the compressed Name TLV. The last Length field of an encoded NameComponent is 0x00 for a name with an even number of components and 0xYF if an odd number of components are present. The process limits a NameComponent TLV to 15 bytes but allows an unlimited number of components. The document's worked example is the name /HAW/Room/481/Humid/99.
sections.plainLanguage: The compression works in three ways. A row of single bits says which optional pieces are present, so their type and length do not have to be written out. Lengths are packed into single bytes using a different number encoding. And the lengths of two name components are squeezed into one byte, four bits each.

sections.title: Stateful Header Compression
sections.content:
ICN LoWPAN employs two orthogonal, stateful compression schemes. Common information shared throughout the local LoWPAN may be memorized in the context state at all nodes and omitted from communication. Second, redundancy in a single Interest-Data exchange may be removed from ICN stateful forwarding on a hop-by-hop basis and memorized in en route state tables.

A Context Identifier is a byte that refers to a particular conceptual context between network devices, and may be used to replace frequently appearing information such as name prefixes, suffixes, or meta information such as Interest lifetime. The 7-bit CID is a locally scoped unique identifier representing the context state shared between the sender and receiver of the frame. If set, the most significant bit indicates the presence of another, subsequent CID byte. The context state is removed from the compressed packet before sending and reinserted after reception, before passing to the upper stack. The actual information in a context and how it is encoded are out of scope, as is the distribution and maintenance of shared context. Frames containing unknown or invalid CIDs MUST be silently discarded.

For en route state, in CCNx and NDN the Name TLV is included in Interest messages and returns in Data messages, where the returning Name TLV either equals the original or contains it as a prefix. ICN LoWPAN reduces this redundancy by replacing Name TLVs with single bytes that represent link-local HopIDs, carried as CIDs of link-local scope. A HopID is valid if not all ID bits are set to zero, which yields 127 distinct HopIDs. If that range is exhausted, messages MUST be sent without en route state compression until new HopIDs are available. A node that forwards without replacing the Name TLV with a HopID MUST invalidate the HopID by setting all ID bits to zero.

While an Interest is traversing the network, a forwarder generates an ephemeral HopID tied to a Pending Interest Table entry. Each HopID MUST be unique within the local PIT and exists only during the lifetime of a PIT entry. To maintain HopIDs, the local PIT is extended by two new columns, HIDi for inbound HopIDs and HIDo for outbound HopIDs. HopIDs are included in Interests and stored on the next hop with the resulting PIT entry in the HIDi column. The HopID is replaced with a newly generated local HopID before the Interest is forwarded, and this new HopID is stored in the HIDo column of the local PIT.

Responses include the HopIDs that were obtained from Interests. If the returning Name TLV equals the original, the name is entirely elided; otherwise only the matching name prefix is elided and the distinct suffix is included along with the HopID. When a response is forwarded, the HopID is extracted and used to match the correct PIT entry by looking it up in the HIDo column, and is then replaced with the corresponding HIDi HopID before the response is forwarded on.

Each forwarder can individually decide whether to take part in en route compression, but a node SHOULD use it whenever the stateful compression mechanism is activated. The PIT extensions are required only at ICN LoWPAN nodes; regular NDN or CCNx forwarders outside an ICN LoWPAN domain do not need them.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of shared memory save more bytes. A context number replaces values that every device in the area already knows, such as a common name prefix. A short HopID replaces the full name in a reply, because the forwarding device remembers which request the reply belongs to, and the reply only has to carry the part of the name that differs.

sections.title: Measured Effect and Deployment Guidance
sections.content:
The scheme has been implemented as an extension of the NDN and CCNx software stack in its IoT version on RIOT, and an experimental evaluation for NDN over ICN LoWPAN with varying configurations has been performed. Energy profiling and processing time measurements indicate significant energy savings, and the amortized costs for processing show no penalties.

The document's theoretical estimate compares the sizes of uncompressed and compressed messages. A typical NDN Interest, containing a CanBePrefix TLV, a MustBeFresh TLV, an InterestLifetime TLV set to 4 seconds and a HopLimit TLV set to 6, is estimated at 21 + 2n + comps_n bytes, where n is the number of name components and comps_n the sum of their lengths. After compression the same Interest is estimated at 10 + n/2 + comps_n bytes. The size difference is 11 + 1.5n bytes. For the name /DE/HH/HAW/BT7 the total size gain is 17 bytes, which is 43 percent of the uncompressed packet.

The compression works best when signed time offsets compress without the need for rounding, when the context state is distributed so that long names can be elided from Interest and Data messages, and when frequently used TLV type numbers stay in the lower range, below 255. Name components are of type GenericNameComponent and are limited to a length of 15 bytes so that compression applies to all messages.

The document asks for further experimental deployments, particularly on name lengths in real deployments such as smart home, smart city and industrial IoT, on the fragmentation scheme, on what else the shared context state could hold, on how the context state could be distributed and synchronized, and on the number of open requests stored in the PIT of memory-constrained devices, since the 127 distinct HopIDs a node can use at once set an upper bound that determines whether the HopID length needs resizing.
sections.plainLanguage: Measured on a real operating system for small devices, the scheme saved energy without adding processing cost. In the worked example the compressed request is 43 percent smaller. The document then lists what is still unknown, such as how long names really are in practice and how the shared context should be distributed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Main memory is typically a scarce resource of constrained networked devices. Fragmentation preserves fragments and purges them only after a packet is reassembled, which requires buffering all fragments. This scheme can handle fragments for distinct packets simultaneously, which can lead to overflowing packet buffers. Implementers are urged to make use of appropriate buffer replacement strategies for fragments, and minimal fragment forwarding can potentially prevent fragment buffer saturation in forwarders.

The stateful header compression generates ephemeral HopIDs for incoming and outgoing Interests and consumes them on returning Data packets. Forged Interests can deplete the number of available HopIDs, thus leading to a denial of compression service for subsequent content requests.

To alleviate the problems caused by forged fragments or Interest initiations, proper protective mechanisms for accessing the link layer should be deployed. IEEE 802.15.4 provides capabilities to protect frames and restrict them to a point-to-point link or a group of devices.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things can go wrong with this scheme on a small device. Reassembling fragmented packets needs memory, and a flood of fake requests can use up the short identifiers the device uses to match replies to requests, so the device stops compressing. Both are handled by careful buffer management and by protecting the radio link.
